summary:
Belgium prohibits discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Same-sex marriage and adoption are legal, and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Under the Law of 25 June 2017, in force since 1 January 2018, transgender people change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, with no medical conditions attached. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the existing procedure.

For minors, the rules are narrower: those aged 12 to 16 may change a first name only, while 16 and 17-year-olds may apply for a sex-marker change with parental consent plus a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

The official Brussels-Capital Region guidance on changing the sex marker on an identity card still lists a medical certificate attesting to a sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, among the requirements. The same page states the change is free of charge, takes three to six weeks, requires a valid identity document, and is applied for in person at the commune, with a digital route available. This regional guidance does not match the federal self-declaration procedure, and the sources do not resolve which requirement a visitor's application would actually encounter.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2,400 euros. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

Violence against LGBTQI people is rising despite the country's progressive legal framework. Equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men reported increasing violence and intimidation in May 2025, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is a dating-app trap: victims are lured by fake profiles to isolated locations and then ambushed, robbed, humiliated or assaulted. An RTBF investigation published in February 2025 found police had recorded an alarming number of such incidents, many unreported through fear or shame. In May 2025 a case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went before the Brussels Criminal Court.

Belgian legislation does not define hate crimes and provides no code to record them as such; conduct that breaches non-discrimination law but constitutes a criminal offence is prosecuted under general provisions instead. The one conviction officially qualified as hate-motivated on sexual-orientation grounds was the 22 December 2014 jury conviction of four people for the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi.

Same-sex couples have held equal adoption rights since 2006 and lesbian couples can access IVF. Until 1 January 2015 the Civil Code automatically recognised the husband of a biological mother as father while a mother's female partner had to complete an adoption procedure; a bill approved in 2014 corrected this.

Recorded harassment remains widespread: a 2019 study found 90% of LGBT people in Brussels had suffered verbal or psychological harassment, and a 2018 human rights body count recorded 125 homophobic discrimination cases, including 17 physical attacks, 42 public insults, 17 housing cases and 31 online attacks.
tangentialFactors:
Belgium adopted Europe's first femicide law in 2023, covering all gender-based homicide, which places gender-motivated killing under a dedicated statutory frame rather than general homicide provisions.

State hostility toward LGBT people is essentially absent at the level of major institutions, but right-wing political hostility has a record. The Flemish Block and later Vlaams Belang voted against same-sex marriage; the party's leader stated in 2015 that it would not campaign to repeal same-sex marriage, and in 2019 its chairman condemned an MP who criticised same-sex marriage and adoption after public outcry. N-VA was criticised for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores Belgium across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum and intersex categories, giving a formal-law comparison point against the enforcement picture above.

Trans visibility in public life has been high: transgender journalist Bo Van Spilbeeck's 2018 coming-out received widespread coverage, and a 2017 survey study by the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men, 'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later', documented obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, and related problems at work and in economic status.

Travel-industry guides describe Belgium as one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers, with a thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège. That framing is marketing copy and sits alongside the documented rise in assaults.
localsOnly:
The gender-marker change is applied for at the commune, is free of charge and takes three to six weeks according to the Brussels-Capital Region page, which also offers a digital route. The federal procedure is a declaration to the civil registrar with no medical conditions attached.

The 2017 law was framed by Justice Minister Koen Geens around self-determination, with all medical conditions including sterilisation and surgery scrapped, and it includes a reflection period and public-order safeguards. Name-change requests rose from 85 in 2012 to 187 in 2016.

Reporting routes for discrimination and hate incidents run through Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men, the bodies that published the 2025 caseload figures. The OSCE/ODIHR national framework page notes that because hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation, such cases are handled under general criminal provisions.

Family formation is settled in law: same-sex couples have held the same adoption rights as opposite-sex couples since 2006, and 70 LGBT domestic adoptions were recorded between 2006 and 2014, comprising 58 male couples and 2 female couples in Flanders plus 12 adoptions in the French Community.

Support infrastructure for trans people includes the Flemish Ministry of Health-funded suicide prevention project lumi.be and the dedicated transgender youth site gendervonk.be, both launched in 2019.

Sex between men has been legal since 1795 under the French penal code, and the age of consent has been equal at 16 regardless of sexual orientation since then; article 372bis raised it to 18 for same-sex acts between 1965 and 1985 and was repealed on 18 June 1985.

The Unia caseload of 136 cases is counted by sexual orientation, and the statement that trans people are especially affected comes from the equality bodies' general reporting rather than a trans-specific dataset.
